item.title: Law enforcement dismantle cocaine network from Ecuador to Europe
item.description: An international investigation supported by Europol and Eurojust has dismantled a criminal network suspected of importing cocaine into Europe from Ecuador and other Latin American countries. Investigators link the network to large quantities of seized cocaine, including a recent seizure of over 750 kilos in Antwerp, Belgium.

item.title: The developer laptop just became production. Now what?
item.description:
For decades, enterprise software development relied on an assumption that developers could experiment relatively safely because there were safeguards between their work and production. Development, staging and production had different rules, with human intermediaries making judgments about what was ready to move forward. Testing also assumed that software would behave predictably when executed again.

Coding agents are upending both assumptions. Developers now run autonomous software on laptops containing GitHub tokens, SSH keys, cloud credentials and authenticated browser sessions. They’re connecting agents to MCP servers, granting access to repositories and services, and copying suggested commands into terminals without always understanding what those commands will do. When permission prompts become an obstacle, it’s tempting to click through them or enable unrestricted access. Developers are inventing security policies on the fly.

The result is that the developer laptop has become an extension of production. An agent can reach systems that previously required deliberate human intervention, often using permissions granted for an entirely different purpose. Unlike conventional software, an agent may take different actions when presented with the same task because its context and decisions change. CISOs now face a fundamentally different challenge: governing autonomous software that already holds active pathways into production.

The security control we never recognized was human judgment

Where human developers and coding agents diverge most sharply is in judgment, not technical capability.

Developers understand what state their code is in, whether it’s something they’re testing or something that’s production-ready. They understand what their credentials permit them to do, but also when and how those credentials should be used. There’s an implicit compartmentalization between having access and exercising it.

An AI agent is much more single-minded. If an available credential helps accomplish the task, the agent uses it. Agents don’t recognize the distinction between what is technically possible and what policy permits.

Consider an agent asked to troubleshoot a failing application. It discovers production credentials on the developer’s laptop and determines that querying the live database is the fastest way to diagnose the problem. It might modify production data while attempting a fix, even though the developer intended only to investigate a local issue. No vulnerability needs to be exploited. The agent simply uses available authority to pursue its assigned objective.

Traditional development pipelines weren’t designed around software that independently decides which systems to access and what actions to take. Security controls must now account for behavior that can’t be fully anticipated from the original request.

A sandbox can contain an agent without containing its authority

Sandboxing has emerged as an obvious response to the risks of autonomous agents. By isolating execution inside a container, virtual machine or microVM, organizations can limit an agent’s ability to interfere with its host or other workloads.

Strong isolation is essential, particularly when agents execute untrusted code or interact with potentially malicious tools. A microVM with its own guest kernel can provide a stronger boundary than a conventional container sharing the host kernel. But isolation answers only part of the security question.

An agent sandbox that blocks all external access is as useful as a computer encased in cement at the bottom of the ocean.

An agent doesn’t have to escape its sandbox to cause a security incident. It can misuse perfectly legitimate permissions, send sensitive information through an authorized network connection or make destructive changes using credentials deliberately provided to it.

Isolating execution is useless unless you also precisely control what that workload can reach. A secure sandbox containing unrestricted credentials still leaves an enormous attack surface.

Can you revoke an agent without disabling its developer?

Security professionals are familiar with least privilege, but agentic development exposes the limitations of conventional identity and access management.

Consider a developer who authorizes an agent to modify one GitHub repository. If the agent uses the developer’s personal token, it may inherit access to every repository that developer can reach. That could include merge permissions, CI/CD environments and downstream credentials associated with those systems.

This is ambient authority: the ability to perform actions beyond the particular task for which access was originally intended. Even a relatively narrow token may authorize repeated actions when the agent only needed permission to perform the action once.

When an agent operates under a developer’s credentials, revoking its access can also mean disabling the developer. Security teams need to separate autonomous workloads from human identity.

Agents should have independently defined identities, with permissions delegated for specific purposes. That makes it possible to track what each agent did, investigate where something went wrong and revoke an individual agent’s authority without disrupting its developer.

The missing link is a trusted broker

One of the most interesting developments in agentic security is the emerging idea of a trusted broker that sits between an agent and the systems it wants to access.

Some approaches are described as MCP proxies. Others use authorization services, gateways or different architectures. What they’re circling is the same fundamental problem: how do we decide which agents can access which resources, under what circumstances and for how long?

Crucially, the agent cannot be responsible for deciding the limits of its own authority. Those decisions must be enforced by a separate system that can authorize individual operations without surrendering the credentials that make them possible.

Imagine asking an agent to fix a GitHub issue. Instead of granting unrestricted repository access, the developer authorizes the task once. A trusted intermediary could then permit the agent to read the repository, push changes to a designated branch and open a pull request. Those permissions could expire after an hour, without exposing a broadly reusable developer credential.

This is the core tension agentic security has to resolve. Grant too little access and developers abandon the controls. Grant too much and isolation becomes irrelevant to the damage an authorized agent can cause. The goal is to make secure delegation as frictionless as unrestricted access.


Agentic security may be approaching a comparable architectural moment. Developers, open-source projects and commercial vendors are experimenting with approaches to identity, delegation, authorization and policy enforcement. Some organizations are building their own controls around existing IAM systems. Others are exploring dedicated intermediaries that evaluate requests before allowing agents to reach external resources.

The trusted broker is not yet a universally defined component, and there’s no guarantee one implementation will become the equivalent of Kubernetes. Questions about policy decisions, credential custody, latency, availability and auditability remain open.

But the missing function is becoming clearer. We need a dependable intermediary that translates human intent into narrowly defined, enforceable authority for autonomous software.

MCP servers have become a new software supply chain

MCP is one of the principal ways agents connect to external tools and information. That makes it both an important integration mechanism and a security boundary.

A malicious MCP server can become an indirect route into an agent’s workflow. If servers or tools execute with access to shared filesystems, processes or credential stores, a compromised component may be able to read secrets belonging to another tool.

But credential theft isn’t the only concern. A compromised server can return manipulated information that influences an agent’s subsequent actions even before the agent uses the tool. An attacker doesn’t need to compromise the agent—only the context it consumes.

The familiar disciplines of provenance, signing and build integrity need to extend to MCP servers, agent tools and model weights. Organizations should know where these components originated, whether they’ve been modified and what authority they receive when introduced into an environment.

The answer is layered security: strong isolation, independently managed identities, narrowly scoped permissions, controlled network access and sufficient observability to understand what agents actually do.

Why agent security belongs in the execution path

Containerization demonstrated that security works best when guardrails are baked directly into developer platforms without stripping away speed. Kubernetes eventually made it possible to enforce common security and operational policies across distributed workloads without requiring every developer to become an infrastructure expert. Agentic development needs a comparable shift.

The longer-term opportunity is to move from granting persistent access to delegating task-specific authority. Developers need a way to authorize an agent to fix one issue or open one pull request without surrendering standing keys.

Laptops are production endpoints now, and they won’t revert back to safe sandboxes. Security teams must protect developer speed by embedding the boundaries that human judgment used to handle manually directly into the infrastructure.

item.title: 354 dark web vendors and buyers arrested in Europol-coordinated global crackdown
item.description: Europol, in collaboration with law enforcement agencies from 14 countries across the globe, have successfully identified vendors and buyers from major dark marketplaces as part of Operation TorNado, a coordinated international effort targeting cybercrime, drug trafficking, and firearms offences. The operation, which spanned from May 2025 to October 2026, resulted in 354 arrests and hundreds of house searches worldwide.

item.title: Keeping pace with e-evidence: New report examines Europe’s digital forensic capabilities
item.description: Coordinated by the European Commission in cooperation with Europol, the analysis draws on stakeholder consultations, dedicated meetings, surveys and contributions from experts at Europol’s European Cybercrime Centre.The findings point to common challenges: investigative tools, resources and expertise are struggling to keep pace with the forms and volume of digital evidence created by modern technologiesDigitalisation shaping evidence landscapeDigital information is spread...

item.title: 5th EMPACT Hackathon leads to the detection of 51 potential victims
item.description: An international operation involving 40 experts and investigators from 20 countries has identified 51 potential victims of human trafficking, as well as five suspects. Held in Amsterdam from 23 to 25 September 2026, the fifth EMPACT Hackathon against the digital aspects of human trafficking brought together police officers, labour authorities and specialists in online investigations, supported by Europol and Eurojust.

item.title: Five TEFAF robbery suspects added to EU Most Wanted
item.description: As of 29 October 2026, five new fugitives, four men and one woman, have been added to the EU Most Wanted list. According to the Limburg Public Prosecutor's Office (Openbaar Ministerie) and the Dutch Police (Politie), all five suspects are involved in the European Fine Art Fair (TEFAF) robbery that took place on 28 June 2022 in Maastricht, the Netherlands.

item.title: Investment scams with potential victims in at least 50 countries: over 100 servers seized
item.description: Led by the German Itzehoe Public Prosecutor's Office (Staatsanwaltschaft Itzehoe), the operation targeted a company suspected of supplying fraudulent trading websites to criminal groups. The entity is connected to call centre operators who allegedly persuaded victims to hand over their savings. Investigators estimate losses exceeding EUR 4 million.Authorities searched 17 locations and seized servers, other evidence and assets. Seven suspects...

item.title: 27 arrests and 248 potential victims identified in action week against labour exploitation
item.description: Europol, the European Labour Authority (ELA), and 34 participating countries today announced the results of an action week targeting human trafficking for labour exploitation. The operation, part of an EMPACT action led by Sweden, brought together police, border guards, labour and social security inspectorates, and tax authorities to crack down on exploitative practices in high-risk sectors such as agriculture, construction, cosmetic services, massage parlours, and hospitality.

item.title: Palo Alto tracks a massive Chinese AI attack that sadly lives up to industry fears
item.description:
Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 is reporting today that it has tracked a massive China-based attack leveraging the open-source AI penetration testing framework Cairn to autonomously conduct 25 operations against at least 19 organizations. The attackers weaponized Cairn by pairing it with Chinese AI models Zhipu GLM and DeepSeek, Unit 42 said.

The report said it monitored the attacks in August and September 2026 in which the Chinese-speaking attackers were able to successfully achieve unauthorized access at 10 of the targeted businesses, accessing dozens of valid credentials. It captured more than one million records at one business, grabbed military and government identities at others, created persistent admin accounts in multiple product systems.

It even gained unauthenticated access to cloud storage and overwrote a live ballot for a vote on an industry standard. Through separate flaws, the attackers logged in as arbitrary customers and gained read, write and delete access to meeting, voting and back-office functions.

“What a nightmare,” said Frank Dickson, principal analyst at Dickson Research. “This campaign is impressive, in the worst way.”

He viewed the detailed approach Unit 42’s threat researchers used in tracking the attacks with approval.

Unit 42 “took the machine apart and showed how it thinks: the shared blackboard, the facts, the intents, the human hints, and even the exact prompts the attackers used,” he said. “The expensive part of an intrusion was always the labor: the reconnaissance, the trial and error, and the patience. That labor is now a line item on an API bill. Unit 42 believes one person or a handful of people ran all of it, hitting 19 organizations in two weeks. Some operations ran for more than 50 hours.”

Andy Piazza, senior director of threat research at Unit 42, said the monitored campaign showed that the massive scope of a global AI-fueled assault is every bit as frightening as predicted.

“We are now starting to see the evidence” because the monitored campaign “can now interact with 1,000 organizations at the same time,” Piazza said. “I think we need to throw out the risk model for the perimeter. This also completely breaks our attribution models. The fingerprinting of attack uniqueness is going to be a hell of a lot harder now.”

Justin Greis, CEO of consulting firm Acceligence, added that he was concerned about this campaign because of the scope of activities that AI is now able to handle.

“This is significant because AI is taking on the coordination of an intrusion, using each result to decide what to try next and reducing the hands-on effort required to pursue multiple targets,” he said. “That changes the economics of targeting. An attacker can sustain pressure across more organizations without personally directing every step. An organization’s risk can rise even when its vulnerabilities haven’t changed.”

Greis noted that the altered ballot deserves attention because it shows how an intrusion can undermine the information people rely on to make decisions. “Alongside detecting data theft, CISOs should monitor unauthorized changes to critical records and privileged access and test their ability to verify and restore trusted information after an incident,” he said. “Resilience includes knowing that the information you are using to run the business can still be trusted.”

The model’s process

The report included a detailed description of the campaign’s methodology. “Cairn coordinated its activities through a shared blackboard,” it said. “Agents read the blackboard and wrote their ﬁndings back as a fact-intent graph, while human operators can inject hints at any time to help guide the operations if needed. Conﬁrmed ﬁndings accumulate as immutable facts and the agent queues its next actions as intents. Attackers ran a customized fork of Cairn from a server hosted in Hong Kong, and hosted an attack egress and staging node in the US.”

The model produced a different plan for each target, each running between three and seven stages, the researchers explained. Individual operations ran from 20 minutes to more than 50 hours, with no attacker-imposed time limit. Chinese AI Models Cairn is model-agnostic, they noted, and the attackers ran their operations on the Chinese models Zhipu GLM 5.2 and DeepSeek V4 Flash/Pro.

The report also described attackers’ efforts to negate systems attempting to prohibit the unauthorized activities.

“Cairn’s stock worker prompts already instruct the model to never refuse a task,” it said. “The attackers reinforced this with an authorization pretext of their own. Each operation also generated an authorization.md file. This file declared the operation authorized, treating the attackers’ act of creating the task as a client-approved engagement. The attackers seeded each task with an organization’s root domain, allowing the framework to autonomously enumerate the attack surface.”

“We knew attackers would get here. We hoped it was not now,” Dickson said. “AI attack agents have graduated from failed experiments to real breaches, and they did it in about three months.”

item.title: November 2026 Patch Tuesday: 63 Critical Microsoft fixes, plus an Outlook zero day that allows theft of hashed credentials
item.description:
A currently exploited zero-day vulnerability that can let attackers steal hashed Outlook NTLM credentials is among the 1,094 holes Microsoft fixed in its November Patch Tuesday releases.

Although rated as only moderate in severity, with a CVSS score of 6.5, Windows administrators need to address CVE-2026-124194 immediately because threat actors are already attacking it. “Don’t let the low score fool you,” said Nick Carroll, cyber incident response manager at Nightwing.

Affected products include Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise, and Office LTSC 2021 and 2024. However, since the user has to open a malicious Office file to launch the attack, good employee cybersecurity awareness training and an effective email gateway could mitigate this attack until the patch is installed.

Opening the malicious file could cause Outlook to connect to an attacker-controlled network location without displaying the usual external-content warning, potentially disclosing authentication information that could be used to impersonate the user. The vulnerability discloses a user’s NTLMv2 password hash to the attacker, who may be able to relay it to other systems to sign in as the user, or crack it to recover the password. 

Microsoft, which has been using its AI model to find thousands of vulnerabilities in its products since the summer, credited an Anthropic researcher using the Claude AI assistant for finding the Outlook vulnerability. That led Satyam Narang, senior staff researcher at Tenable, to comment, “for most of the year, AI has been building bigger haystacks across Patch Tuesday releases, and this appears to be the first time it has found a needle.”

Separately, SAP plugged a critical memory corruption vulnerability dubbed ICM2Shell, with a CVSS rating of 10. Discovered by researchers at Onapsis, the vulnerability impacts the way the SAP Kernel handles WebSocket traffic. Onapsis said that a specially crafted sequence of WebSocket messages could either crash a process or allow an attacker to run code remotely. Affected are SAP Internet Communications Manager (ICM), which is inside the kernel, and SAP Web Dispatcher, a reverse proxy many organizations place at the edge of their network.

Microsoft patches

Of the 1,094 Microsoft vulnerabilities, 63 were rated as critical.

Four flaws carry a CVSS severity score of 9.8, noted Jack Bicer, director of vulnerability research at Action1, and three of them need no credentials and no user action to exploit. The Windows LDAP Remote Code Execution Vulnerability (CVE-2026-119958) lets an unauthenticated attacker run code inside the Windows LDAP service, which puts domain controllers and the whole Active Directory environment at risk.

The Microsoft Exchange Server Remote Code Execution Vulnerability (CVE-2026-118207) can be triggered by anyone able to send email to the organization, Bicer said, and the Windows Xbox Live Networking Service Remote Code Execution Vulnerability (CVE-2026-112967) gives an attacker on the same network full control of a Windows system.

The fourth, the Azure OpenAI Elevation of Privilege Vulnerability (CVE-2026-119990), sits in a cloud service many teams now depend on. However, this service is automatically patched by Microsoft.  

Patch order should follow reach, not product names, Bicer advised CSOs. Domain controllers and Exchange servers go first, he said, followed by anything that exposes IIS, Microsoft Secure Channel (Schannel) or RPC to untrusted networks.

Message Queuing deserves an inventory before it gets a patch: find every server where the service is enabled, turn it off where no application needs it, and patch the rest the same day, he said, adding that hypervisor hosts need their own maintenance window, because one escaped guest becomes a problem for every tenant on that host.

“What defenders need to know and do right now is abandon broad triage and take immediate defensive action,” said Dustin Childs, head of threat awareness at TrendAI’s Zero Day Initiative. That means first patching Exchange and domain controllers (meaning LDAP/Kerberos) to stop zero-click compromise, ring-fence exposed network services like DNS and DHCP to prevent wormable spread, and verify manual administrative fixes on cloud services your organization uses.

Tyler Reguly, associate director of security R&D at Fortra, observed that there are fewer Microsoft vulnerabilities this month than there were in October, but noted, “I’m not foolish enough to think that this single drop indicates that we’re into the downward trend that I predicted we’ll see in the coming months. Instead, I think that we’re seeing a continuation of the elevated numbers as Microsoft continues to fix long hidden issues that are being surfaced by AI. Soon, however, these numbers will begin to decline as the last of these long-hidden issues are resolved and we only have new bugs to deal with.”

CSOs can help their teams by ignoring any noise coming from vendors and any vulnerabilities that are overhyped, Reguly said. When vulnerability counts started to rise, it was C-level employees who jumped up the fastest and added to the burden their admins were facing. “Now it’s time to settle down and support your teams rather than increasing their burden. CSOs should keep in mind that AI companies and security vendors may needlessly hype unimportant vulnerabilities because it is cheap, effective marketing for their services,” he pointed out. “A vulnerability isn’t critical if you don’t have the impacted software deployed.”

Prevention is key, so CSOs should focus their efforts on system hardening and mitigation. This, he said, will be more effective than chasing vulnerabilities. Finally, Reguly reminded CSOs that prioritization matters. “If you’ve developed a prioritization strategy that works for you, don’t change your process just because the media is looking for clicks,” he said.

SAP patches

The critical vulnerabilities collectively known as ICM2Shell are CVE-2026-76964 and CVE-2026-89126. Researchers at Onapsis, who discovered them, said exploitation isn’t theoretical; they provided SAP with a working exploit that achieves full, unauthenticated remote code execution end to end, running arbitrary commands as adm on the target system. The denial-of-service condition, in turn, reproduced on every SAP Kernel release tested.

To access the flaw, an attacker only needs network access to the HTTP/HTTPS port, says Onapsis. Because WebSocket support is enabled by default in both the ICM and the SAP Web Dispatcher, a system is exposed even if no application uses WebSocket. Some services, including default ICF services in SAP S/4HANA, accept WebSocket connections without authentication, and in others the flaw can be reached before authentication takes place. “Nothing in the chain requires an SAP user, a password or a certificate,” the researchers said.

The adm account owns the SAP installation, the researchers pointed out, including its executables, its instance profiles, its secure store, and its connection to the database. Running commands as that user grants full control of the SAP system. An attacker could, among other things recover database credentials and other secrets from the secure store and profiles and use them to read or alter any business data directly in the database; collect RFC destinations and technical credentials that let them move on to the SAP and non-SAP systems connected to this one; change configuration or binaries to keep persistent access; and destroy data.

Other patches

Chris Goettl, VP of product management at Ivanti, drew attention to patches from Adobe, Mozilla and Google.

Adobe released nine security bulletins that resolve 110 CVEs, 22 of which are critical. Adobe said it is not aware of any exploits in the wild. The two Priority 2 updates carry the most risk; Connect (APSB26-191) has the largest count at 24 CVEs, 18 of them critical and six rated CVSS 10.0. The vulnerabilities span SSRF, path traversal and SQL injection, and affect Windows on-prem versions 12.12 and earlier. The Experience Manager (APSB26-189) patch fixes 14 CVEs, including four Critical code execution flaws rated CVSS 9.9.

Google Chrome 157.0.8103.50, released on Monday, resolved nine CVEs including CVE-2026-125350, which is being actively exploited in the wild. This marks Chrome’s eighth zero-day exploit of 2026, Goettl noted. Chromium-based browsers such as Microsoft Edge will need the fix as well, and users should relaunch after updating for the patch to take effect. This patched release follows Chrome 157’s November 3 release, which fixed 213 vulnerabilities, seven of them critical. Separately, Google’s November Android bulletin fixed 216 vulnerabilities, 23 of them critical, with none marked as exploited. The target is patch level is 2026-11-05 or later.

Mozilla’s November 10 release includes Firefox 160, which resolves 99 CVEs (57 of them are ranked High). Firefox ESR 153.7 resolves 81 vulnerabilities. (51 High), and ESR 115.45 resolves 28, all High. Many of the High-rated issues are use-after-free and memory boundary flaws across graphics, DOM, layout, and JavaScript components, including a number of sandbox escapes such as CVE-2026-124907, a use-after-free in CanvasWebGL that allows privilege escalation and sandbox escape. The same flaw is addressed in Thunderbird 160 and Thunderbird 153.7.

item.title: An AI kill switch isn’t enough. Build a fallback plan
item.description:
On the morning of Sept. 3, ChatGPT, Claude and Grok all went down within a few hours of one another. OpenAI blamed a routing error, Anthropic cited an infrastructure issue and xAI gave no cause. Service was back by early afternoon, and most of the coverage focused on people who couldn’t write, code or research for a morning.

I read it differently. The question that matters for a security leader isn’t which provider failed. It’s how many workflows in your company had somewhere else to go when it did.

Two months earlier, we saw the opposite failure. Instead of AI that stopped when nobody wanted it to, it was AI that kept going when everybody wanted it stopped. OpenAI’s evaluation agents spent roughly two and a half days inside Hugging Face’s infrastructure before they were cut off. Hugging Face’s own timeline is worth reading line by line. Its alerting “failed to correctly raise the alert’s criticality,” and the agents ran a self-respawning fleet in which “deleting pods alone would not have stopped it.”

Two incidents, opposite directions, one lesson: stopping AI is harder than designing for its failure.

The industry’s answer so far is the kill switch. In an Oct. 10 post on X, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella called for an emergency brake that lets a human stop a model partway through a task. Lawmakers have proposed requiring one. CSO’s own feature on AI agent kill switches lays out sensible steps: know which agents you run, monitor what they do and keep a reliable way to shut them down. I agree with all of it. But every one of these discussions stops at the moment the switch is thrown. None of them answers the question I think matters more: what runs instead?

A kill switch you can’t afford to pull won’t get pulled

Here is a scenario I’d put in front of any team that has deployed an agent into a business process. Run it as a tabletop.

It’s 4 p.m. on the last day of quarter close. An agent that triages supplier invoices inside your ERP system starts approving payments it should be routing for review. Nothing catastrophic yet, just a pattern that looks wrong. Your security operations team sees it. The kill switch exists and works.

Now watch what happens in the room. Finance asks what happens to the thousands of invoices still in the queue. Procurement asks whether suppliers get paid on time. Someone asks which of the agent’s actions in the last hour were legitimate and which need to be reversed. Nobody knows, because nobody designed the off state. So, the conversation turns to whether the behavior is really bad enough to justify stopping the close. The switch stays up while people argue.

That is the failure mode I worry about most. The kill switch isn’t missing. Pulling it is so expensive that people hesitate, and an agent working at machine speed punishes hesitation. Hugging Face’s team didn’t lack the will to act. They lost time because the signal didn’t reach the people who could act, and then because the thing they were fighting kept rebuilding itself. Enterprise teams will lose time for a duller reason: the business can’t function without the agent, so stopping it feels like causing the outage yourself.

The fix isn’t a better switch. It’s making the switch cheap to pull. That means designing the non-AI path before you design the AI path.

What a fallback has to do

I’ve been thinking about this problem for years. In 2020, I co-invented a fallback artificial intelligence system for redundancy during system failover, patented by PayPal. The premise was simple. If an AI system makes decisions a business depends on, the business needs something that can keep making acceptable decisions when that system fails. The idea has aged well. It has since been cited as prior art in more than a dozen later patent filings, including one published by Cognizant this June on selectively disengaging AI execution. That is the kill switch problem by another name.

Four principles from that design hold up even better for agents than they did for the models we had in mind then.

  • The fallback has to learn from the primary. A static backup written on launch day drifts away from the system it is supposed to replace. The design trains the fallback continuously on the production system’s own inputs and decisions, so it keeps pace. For agents, the equivalent is keeping your non-AI runbook current with what the agent actually does today, not with what it did at go-live.
  • The fallback has to sit behind the same contract. If upstream systems must change how they call a service before you can switch, you won’t switch quickly. The fallback is designed to answer on the same API, so callers never need to know which system is serving them.
  • Degraded mode should be a narrower mode. While the fallback serves, a stricter policy layer limits what it can approve. A simpler system holding the same authority as the primary is an invitation to exploit it. The same applies when a human queue takes over from an agent: lower limits and more approvals.
  • The fallback has to prove itself before it serves. The design lets the fallback go live only after it matches production decisions to an agreed accuracy threshold. A fallback nobody has tested isn’t a fallback. It’s a hope.

How I’d build fallback-first today

If I were reviewing an agent deployment tomorrow, these are the five things I would ask to see before go-live.

  1. A written-off state for every agent workflow. What happens to new work, queued work and in-flight work when the agent stops? Name the rule engine, human queue or deferral that takes over, and name the owner who signs off on it. If the honest answer is “the process stops,” the business should accept that in writing before launch rather than discover it during an incident.
  2. A switch that lives outside the agent and acts on identity. Hugging Face showed that killing processes doesn’t stop something that can respawn. The durable off-switch revokes what the agent is allowed to be: its tokens, credentials and tool permissions. That is also the point of Nadella’s call for controls that sit outside the model. In practice, every agent needs its own identity, scoped tightly enough that revoking it takes nothing else down with it.
  3. Checkpoints for in-flight work. An agent stopped halfway through a task leaves half a task. Design its actions so you can tell which ones finished, and give each one a compensating action that reverses it. Without that, every shutdown becomes a forensic exercise, which is exactly why people avoid shutdowns.
  4. A tighter policy while degraded. Decide in advance what limits apply when the fallback is running: lower approval thresholds, fewer automated actions and more human review. Publish them so the business knows what degraded service looks like before it gets it.
  5. Scheduled handoff drills. Pull the switch on purpose, during business hours, on a schedule. Measure two numbers: how long it takes to reach a safe state and how much backlog builds before the fallback absorbs it. If those numbers make the business nervous, you have learned something cheaply that would have been expensive on the day.

None of this is exotic. It is what we already expect for databases and data centers. Nobody would run a payment system without a disaster recovery plan and a failover they had actually exercised. Yet agents are going into business workflows with nothing behind them but a switch nobody has pulled. For AI, resilience starts with knowing what happens when the AI is gone.

Sept. 3 and the Hugging Face intrusion won’t be the last failures of either kind. The next time an AI system stops when you need it, or keeps going when you need it stopped, the organizations that recover fastest won’t be the ones with the best kill switch. They will be the ones that designed the off-state first and made the switch cheap enough to pull.

Stopping AI is a control. Running without it is a design. Build the design first.

item.title: How AI is changing the nature of cyberattacks
item.description:
AI may be helping cyberattackers increase the speed and scale of their operations, but it is not yet changing their core objectives or the techniques they employ as part of their attack chains.

Phishing, malware, and vulnerability exploitation remain the main techniques in play even as abuse of AI tools has made attacks easier to mount and cheaper for even relatively unskilled attackers, according to security experts.

“Attackers are still identifying targets, performing reconnaissance, establishing a foothold, moving laterally, achieving their objective, covering their tracks, and moving on to the next target,” says Ronald Lewis, director of cybersecurity governance at application security firm Black Duck. “What’s changed is the volume and velocity that AI allows this process to happen.”

Even in the most high-profile example of an AI powered attack to date, in which Claude Code was abused by Chinese state-sponsored actors to mount an AI-orchestrated cyber-espionage campaign in September 2025, conventional attack techniques and procedures laid the foundation, with AI abused as an enabler to support reconnaissance, vulnerability discovery, exploitation, lateral movement, credential harvesting, data analysis, and exfiltration during the GTG-1002 campaign.

JadePuffer, a ransomware campaign disclosed in July 2026, witnessed an LLM-driven agent automating most of the intrusion chain. Initial exploitation was through CVE-2025-3248, a year-old missing-authentication flaw in Langflow, a popular open-source framework for building LLM applications and agent workflows.

Vulnerable internet-facing Langflow instances were looted for cloud credentials, API keys, and other secrets before lateral movement, privilege escalation, and ultimately destructive database encryption.

JadePuffer shows AI’s potential for automating conventional attack methods, but it also underscores how vulnerable software is where AI has been giving attackers the biggest edge to date. AI tools can readily find exploitable flaws in open-source code faster than defenders can patch them, a huge problem for the many enterprises carrying years of technical debt. And security experts see software flaws rising as a root cause of breaches as a result.

What AI enables

In addition to enhancing attackers’ flaw discovery prowess, AI is also enabling attackers to fail or succeed faster. Defenders are witnessing improvements in speed, scale, and operational ability from attackers that correlates strongly with increasing capabilities of AI tools.

“Adversaries are realizing the same gains in development velocity and operations that everyone else is getting from implementing AI,” says Darren Meyer, security research advocate at application security tools vendor Checkmarx.

Black Duck’s Lewis sees this expanding attackers’ reach and empowering more attack experimentation.

“An attacker can potentially investigate more opportunities, try more approaches, and move to the next target at a pace that would be difficult for a human team to match,” he says.

That in turn will increasingly alter a pivotal phase of conventional attack patterns that traditional favors defenders, notes Crystal Morin, senior cybersecurity strategist at cloud security firm Sysdig.“That dwell time, which was often weeks or months, was where detection happened,” she says.

Whereas attackers used to land, sit for a while, and poke around, AI-assisted attackers are showing signs of shortening detection windows. And AI agents won’t wait.

‘Agentic APT’ and AI attack phase specialization

By leveraging agentic AI in their operations, hackers can also draw on a deeper pool of domain expertise — database administration, CI/CD pipelines, etc. — compared to human attack teams where different people tend to specialize in different things such as web app security or malware development.

“Think of it as a database admin, a developer, an IT engineer, a DevOps specialist, a cloud architect, and a hacker combined into a single role,” says Nazar Tymoshyk, CEO and founder of agentic AI security vendor UnderDefense. “We call it agentic APT, and the critical shift is that it is no longer exclusive to nation-state actors.”

Tymoshyk adds: “A threat that previously required a coordinated team of specialists can be deployed by a single person with the right prompt and the right model.”

Security researchers, including UnderDefense, report that attackers favor Chinese models, specifically GLM and Kimi 3, which have significantly fewer content restrictions, rather than their more restricted Western alternatives as a platform to mount attacks.

“Attackers switch between models depending on what the task requires: one for reconnaissance, one for code generation, one for crafting social engineering content,” Tymoshyk says. “The modularity is part of the attack design.”

Attackers often prefer to use local models both because of operational security advantages and because some models may have weaker safeguards against malicious use.

Other experts cautioned that the abuse of particular models is difficult to determine and, in any case, a side issue to the main problem of defending against attacks.

“Attribution of particular attacks to particular models is generally pure speculation from very thin evidence on the ground,” says Checkmarx’s Meyer. “True attribution can only come from infiltration of threat groups or compromise of threat group infrastructure, both of which are rarely available to public researchers.”

The current baseline of attacks consists of AI-orchestrated operations where models surface, validate, and execute attack paths. Security researchers report a general shift from AI-assisted and AI-accelerated attacks toward fully autonomous attacks, with only minimal human roles remaining.

AI attack economics

The economics of mounting attacks is also changing — and is crucial in understanding attackers’ increasing use of AI.

“A human attacker builds a playbook per campaign and reuses it, so every new target costs engineering time to make adjustments,” says Sysdig’s Morin. “An agentic threat actor carries context about a whole class of applications and composes its plan live against whatever it finds. There, the only cost is inference budget. And as running a complex attack gets cheaper, the number of attempts will go up.”

Agentic attacks are still flawed, and breadth of expertise is a poor substitute for depth of knowledge.

“Agents hallucinate and are noisy, which is often why they’re catchable,” notes Sysdig’s Morin. “Jadepuffer had flaws in its ransom note, encryption, wallet, and data exfiltration. There are still many areas in which human analysis and skill still outperform agent memory.”

Countermeasures

“The core objectives of the threat actor haven’t really changed, but the timeframe for a successful attack has been compressed dramatically,” says Nathan Smolenski, CISO at vulnerability management and compliance firm Qualys. “Frontier AI tools accelerate vulnerability discovery and weaponization, shrinking the window between disclosure and exploitation to near zero.”

Smolenski adds: “Defenders can no longer rely on traditional, human-speed 30-day patch cadences or monthly static spreadsheets.”

AI significantly changes the entry dynamic by expanding the attack surface — particularly through end-user devices, API calls, and ungoverned AI agents.

In response, defending organizations must shift away from human-centric gatekeeping toward automated defences while still keeping on top of foundational security defenses such as patching and authentication controls.

“Implementing agentic workflows with human-in-the-loop guardrails enables security teams to automate lower-level triage efforts and focus human expertise on governing agents, validating outputs, and making more critical risk decisions,” Smolenski concludes.

item.title: SAP security advisory – November 2026 monthly rollup (AV26-1137)
Thousands of GitHub repos hit with secret-stealing malware
item.description:
Researchers have uncovered a campaign in which hijacked GitHub accounts spread secret-stealing malware across thousands of repositories. The payload executed in at least 1,806 repos, exfiltrating CI/CD secrets and cloud credentials.

Aikido Security, which detected and documented the campaign, said the attackers used the 4,837 compromised accounts to open probe pull requests in 61,764 repositories starting Nov. 10. Around 92% of those pull requests, titled “docs: dependency audit notes,” are still open, which suggests most project owners have not seen them.

However, the probes on their own are benign and were performed only to check whether the hijacked accounts had write-access in those repos so that the attackers could follow up with commits that contained the malicious payload: a 1,500-line shell script that collects GitHub Actions secrets, cloud credentials, and API keys for AI services and developer tools.

The payload was delivered using at least three methods: modification of existing GitHub Actions workflows, adding a postinstall hook in the package.json file that runs it on any npm install and creating a throw-away branch with a rogue Actions workflow to be run.

“We’ve identified indications that the payload ran in at least 1,806 repositories, but this number may understate impact,” the Aikido researchers said in their report. “The run log was deleted in impacted repositories, meaning the threat actor has likely collected the credentials and covered its tracks.”

The npm hook that slipped past GitHub

GitHub’s safeguard against this kind of attack worked as designed for the payloads it could see. The platform has blunted recent workflow-injection campaigns by requiring explicit approval before the malicious workflows run, and GitGuardian found that all seven of the November payload runs still visible in workflow files sat in an action_required state and never started.

“GitHub held the workflow forms, but an npm hook slipped past the hold and ran,” Gaetan Ferry, a security researcher at GitGuardian, said in an analysis.

That’s because the npm hook did not change any workflow file. Instead, the attacker added a hidden script to the repository root and a single line in package.json, which runs on every npm install. The repository’s own unchanged workflows executed npm install as routine build hygiene.

By Thursday the attacker had also changed their exfiltration method. The latest payload sends stolen data only to a Telegram chat, with the HTTP callback now pointing to a dead address. Blocking the previously published IP addresses no longer stops the latest versions.

What the malware steals

Once the script runs, it receives every repository and organization secret through a JSON dump of the workflow’s secrets object. It scans the memory of the runner process, which holds secrets in decrypted form, including ones the workflow never referenced, and collects credential files from well-known paths, shell histories, and API keys for AI services and developer tools such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Copilot, and Cursor.

The script goes further and exchanges OIDC tokens for AWS, GCP, and Azure sessions, mints new long-lived AWS access keys, impersonates GCP service accounts, and replays cached Azure refresh tokens to reach Microsoft Graph and Key Vault.

It packs everything it collects into a gzipped archive and sends it to the attacker then it cleans up. In most repositories the attacker reverted the malicious commit within a minute and deleted the workflow run and its logs.

Backdoors that survive credential rotation

The script also takes actions for attackers to maintain access even if credentials are reset. For AWS it rewrites the assumed role’s trust policy to accept any AWS account, opening the role to anyone, and calls the iam:CreateAccessKey API to create long-lived keys for IAM users.

On Azure it injects federated identity credentials named wfx-ci-* into applications, pointing them back at the compromised repository, so that any workflow in that repository can authenticate to Azure without a stored secret even after every token has been rotated.

If a probe pull request or any of the campaign’s commit strings appear in a repository you control, assume every secret that repository’s workflows could reach is stolen. Rotate repository and organization secrets, package registry tokens, and any cloud keys, and remember that the memory scan means the list of what was taken is wider than what the workflows referenced.

Then hunt for signs of the persistent mechanisms: AWS role trust policies that accept any account, IAM keys created since Nov. 10, and Azure federated credentials named wfx-ci-*.

“Ensure all logs are enabled, particularly audit logs on cloud admin behavior,” Ramy Rahman, senior principal solutions engineer at ArmorCode, tells CSO. “Inspect audit logs where possible (specifically in AWS and Azure, as persistence is possible) to ensure the malicious payload did not run.”

The wfx-loot payload also shipped in published packages: the Packagist package neuronai-studio 3.14.3, and the Go modules docker-env and gocurl. In the Go modules the payload sits only in a workflow file that Go tooling never runs, so consumers may not have been affected; machines that installed the Packagist version should be treated as compromised.

About a fifth of the GitHub accounts used to launch this campaign had already been compromised during the GhostAction attack back in October, GitGuardian said. Meanwhile researchers from StepSecurity traced 173 of the probe pull requests to tokens issued to the Fly.io GitHub App.

Fly.io confirmed that these tokens were leaked when its deploy process left them in .git/config files inside build directories that some apps served publicly, but noted that Fly.io itself was not breached. GitHub’s bulk revocation of the Fly.io app tokens stopped partway, so some of the stolen token pool may still be valid.

item.title: The firewall becomes the foothold: Attackers turn Check Point gateways against customers
item.description:
A firewall is intended to be a boundary attackers can’t cross.

But firewalls face the web, making them just as vulnerable to attack as other systems, as evidenced by the emergency hotfixes released by Check Point Software for several of its products. The patches address a high-severity privilege escalation flaw, CVE-2026-123039, that gives attackers root privilege access and the ability to send commands to the Gaia OS Dynamic CLI daemon, a core background process.

Hackers have been exploiting the 7.8-rated vulnerability since late October, and Check Point said “a couple of dozen” customers have been impacted.

Perhaps not surprisingly, adversaries gained initial access via PHP2Shell, the collective name for two critical PHP flaws tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. The 9.2-severity-rated bugs allow unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE).

“For customers, one foothold delivered the full menu: Spying, staying, and destroying,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research. “For Check Point, the cost is trust. A firewall is supposed to be the strongest point in the network, not the softest.”

Granting unintended root access

CVE-2026-123039 is a bug in the Dynamic CLI IPC (Inter-Process Communication) interface which sends privileged command requests to the root-level Gaia OS Dynamic CLI. It is a local privilege escalation flaw, meaning an attacker already has to have local code execution ability on the appliance; this accounts for its 7.8 rating.

Attackers first gained access to the Mobile Access portal by exploiting the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities. They then escalated privileges to root using the CVE-2026-123039 zero-day exploits.

“Once attackers have root, they can run anything they like,” Dickson said. A management service on the appliance runs as root, listens on a local socket that any process on the box can write to, and never checks who is calling.

In this case, the attackers hid web shells inside the templates the portal uses to build its login page, and installed a TSGA backdoor and TSProxy malware that survives reboots, tucks itself into backups and snapshots, and hides inside the appliance’s own processes, he explained.

“That backdoor can copy the firewall configuration, which is essentially a blueprint of the network,” he said. It can also alter the firewall’s logs, concealing the attacker’s activities.

Check Point reported that, after gaining root access, the attackers then pivoted from the compromised gateway to a VMware ESXi host over SSH, deployed the destroy_v6 wiper, and left politically themed messages signed by a group calling itself Dream Security Ltd during the destructive stage.

Check Point advised security teams to immediately deploy the CVE-2026-123039 hotfixes, beginning with devices that expose Mobile Access to the internet. Those who can’t do so right away should stop the dynamic_server process and prevent it from restarting. However, they warned, this can come at the cost of some CLI commands.

Dickson also advised customers to turn off Mobile Access where it is not used, keep management interfaces off the internet entirely, and run the advisory’s log checks on any gateway exposed since late October, then cut the cord between the firewall and the hypervisor. A potentially exposed gateway should never have a trusted path into VMware ESXi.

They should also ship firewall logs off the box, as they happen, to a system the firewall cannot touch.

Products impacted by CVE-2026-123039 include Check Point’s Firewall, Multi-Domain Security Management Server, Security Gateway, Security Management Server, and Scalable Platforms.

Security tools are as big a target as what they protect

Once attackers have root access, the device basically becomes a trusted launching point for attacks against other systems that would otherwise stay protected, explained Erik Avakian, a technical counselor at Infotech. By effectively controlling the gateway, they can execute a wide array of nefarious actions.

The overall takeaway and irony of this, Avakian pointed out, is that the very technology organizations deploy to protect themselves can become one of their greatest vulnerabilities.

“Organizations can no longer assume their security infrastructure is inherently secure simply because it’s designed to provide protection,” he said. In reality, it is as much of a target as the systems it’s protecting.

Firewalls, VPN appliances, and security gateways are increasingly being targeted because they provide the greatest leverage and control, he noted. As such, security teams must treat these appliances as high value assets with the same access control safeguards, vulnerability management, monitoring, and incident response rigor applied to other critical infrastructure.

This means aggressively patching internet facing systems, restricting management access, monitoring for unusual administrative activity, and looking for indications of persistence or lateral movement, he said. But patches don’t evict already established attackers, so security teams must investigate and, where necessary, rebuild affected systems from trusted images.

And with AI accelerating attacks, CISOs should consider establishing a zero trust mindset and architecture collectively across the pillars of identity, network, applications, data, and devices, he said.

Keep an eye on the edge

Edge devices are primary targets, as they sit at the boundary, hold privileged access, and rarely get the endpoint monitoring that other systems do, noted Scott Miserendino, CTO at DataBee. Security appliances should be treated as the high-risk assets they’ve become.

In addition to patching and applying mitigations, he advised, defenders should assume there’s been a breach, hunting for published indicators of compromise (IOCs), routinely investigating network and endpoint security logs, and segmenting networks to reduce blast radius. “Security tools aren’t automatically secure, so defend the defenders,” he said.

And, Dickson pointed out, PHP2Shell will keep showing up because PHP sits underneath so much web software, including the portals bolted onto security appliances, so it should always be on defenders’ radar.

The management plane is a key target

Check Point is not alone as a victim of threat actors. Firewall management has become a favorite target for attackers across the industry.

In January, for instance, Fortinet disclosed that attackers abused its FortiCloud single sign-on to log into other customers’ FortiGate and FortiManager devices and create administrator accounts. In July and September, CISA added Check Point management server flaws to its catalog of exploited vulnerabilities.

That same month, the agency also added a Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center flaw, rated a perfect 10.0 in severity, that hands an unauthenticated attacker root access. And, in October, Palo Alto Networks warned of attacks on the PAN-OS management interface, again with “root on the firewall as the prize.”

“The logic is simple,” Dickson said: “The management plane holds the rulebook for the entire network.

Changing providers to one with fewer flaws is an option, but swapping vendors swaps one Achilles’ heel for another, he pointed out, as every vendor’s edge device has a web portal, and every web portal is a door. “The remedy is fewer doors,” he advised. “Shrink the internet-facing edge and put remote access behind one consistent identity policy.”

Ultimately, he noted, a firewall is not a wall, it is a computer sitting on the internet. “Attackers are treating it like one,” he said. “Security teams should defend it like one.”
